sentences.text: Kentrosaurus is a genus of stegosaurid dinosaur found in the Lindi Region of Tanzania.
It is classified as a small stegosaur.
The animal possessed a long, narrow skull that was small relative to its body size.
Its neck consisted of 13 vertebrae, with the first fused to the skull and the second following it.
The body was covered in extensive bony armor consisting of small plates and spikes of various shapes.
Adult individuals measured approximately 4 to 4.5 meters in length and weighed between 700 and 1600 kilograms.
Some specimens suggest that relatively larger individuals of Kentrosaurus could have existed.
The tail of Kentrosaurus could swing at speeds of up to 50 km/h.
The ratio of robust to gracile femurs was 2:1, suggesting that the more common robust form likely represented females.
The longest spikes on Kentrosaurus were located at the tail end and were used for active defense.
The genus Kentrosaurus was described by the German paleontologist Edwin Hennig in 1915.
The first Kentrosaurus fossils were discovered in 1909, identified as a stegosaur by Werner Janensch in 1910, and formally described by Edwin Hennig in 1915.
Hundreds of Kentrosaurus bones were unearthed by German expeditions in German East Africa between 1909 and 1912.
Hundreds of bones were unearthed by German expeditions in East Africa between 1909 and 1912.
It was a herbivore that swallowed large chunks of fodder with little chewing.
Wear patterns on Kentrosaurus teeth indicate that it ground its food.
Kentrosaurus could feed at heights of up to 1.7 meters while on all fours.
The long tail of Kentrosaurus placed its center of mass unusually far back for a quadrupedal animal.
The straight femora of Kentrosaurus indicate a straight and vertical limb position, unlike typical bipeds.
A 2013 study concluded Kentrosaurus had a higher growth rate than Stegosaurus and Scutellosaurus based on rapid deposition of vascularized bone.
Kentrosaurus likely used its tail spikes to slash attackers or stab soft tissues and break ribs or facial bones.
Earlier researchers suggested Kentrosaurus might have defended itself by charging rearward through attackers like a porcupine.
Based on femur ratios, it is assumed that Kentrosaurus males may have mated with multiple females, a behavior seen in other vertebrates.
Due to armor obstacles, researchers hypothesize Kentrosaurus pairs may have mated back-to-back with the female in a lordosis posture.
The only accepted species of Kentrosaurus is Kentrosaurus aethiopicus, named by Hennig in 1915.
Kentrosaurus has two junior objective synonyms: Kentrurosaurus and Doryphorosaurus.
The genus Kentrosaurus was named by Edwin Hennig in 1915.
In 1993, fragmentary Wyoming fossils named Stegosaurus longispinus by Charles Gilmore in 1914 were classified as a North American species of Kentrosaurus, K. longispinus.
Recent cladistic analyses suggest Kentrosaurus is a derived member of Stegosauria and a close relative of Stegosaurus within the family Stegosauridae.
Kentrosaurus lived during the Late Jurassic period, specifically from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian ages.
Kentrosaurus lived in what is now Tanzania during the Late Jurassic in the Tendaguru Formation.
It is debated whether Kentrosaurus is a primitive or derived member of Stegosauria, with recent analyses suggesting it is more derived and closely related to Stegosaurus.
Some researchers debate whether ridges on Kentrosaurus supported fleshy cheeks instead of a beak.
